planting.note: Set container-grown plants out in spring after the soil has warmed, in humus-rich, well-drained acidic soil sheltered from drying winds.

directions: A western Chinese woodland holly grown mainly in collector arboreta, this slow-growing evergreen produces narrow, spine-edged juvenile leaves that give way to smoother, glossier foliage as the plant ages. Female plants carry small red berries in winter when a male seedling grows nearby for pollination. Give it a sheltered site with dappled shade and consistent moisture, since it resents both waterlogging and prolonged drought. Light pruning in late winter keeps young plants dense before they settle into their eventual small-tree form.

planting.note: Install balled or container stock in spring in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil; allow ample room for its eventual large-shrub to small-tree size.

directions: This East Asian holly carries the largest, glossiest leaves of any commonly cultivated Ilex, each one coarsely toothed and leathery, giving the plant a bold, almost magnolia-like presence in the landscape. Established female specimens are heavy fruiters, holding dull red berry clusters through winter when a male plant grows within pollinating distance. It builds slowly into a dense, broad-headed small tree and tolerates summer heat and humidity better than most large-leaved hollies. Screen or specimen plantings benefit from a deep, well-drained site and occasional watering during extended dry spells.
sources: North Carolina State Extension plant toolbox

planting.note: Plant in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, sheltered woodland soil out of harsh afternoon sun.

directions: Native to woodland margins in Japan, Taiwan, and parts of mainland China, this diminutive hydrangea takes its name from the pale yellow venation visible on its thin, toothed leaves. Flat lacecap flower heads open with small white sterile florets ringing a cluster of tiny fertile blooms in summer. Its compact, twiggy habit suits a shaded border or rock garden rather than a large shrub border, and it prefers consistent moisture over the drought tolerance shown by larger hydrangea species. Light shaping after flowering keeps the plant tidy without sacrificing the following year's bloom.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Set out in spring in moist, well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade in warmer climates.

directions: Found growing on forest margins and streambanks across southern China, Taiwan, and northern Vietnam, this slender-stemmed hydrangea bears flat lacecap flowerheads with a thin ring of white sterile florets surrounding fertile blue-to-white centers in early summer. Its narrow, finely toothed leaves and open, arching habit give it a lighter, more airy look than the common bigleaf hydrangea. It performs best in a cool, humid root zone with protection from strong midday sun, making it a good fit for a shaded woodland planting. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing spent flower stems after bloom.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew Plants of the World Online
